subject: selective
title: Reading test strategies
summary: How the reading comprehension section works, the six main question types, and a step-by-step method for pacing yourself and answering every question.
body:
The reading comprehension section gives you several short texts — a story, an article, a poem, sometimes a poster or cartoon described in words — and asks multiple-choice questions about each one. It is in the selective test because high school subjects expect you to read quickly, understand exactly what a writer says, and work out what they mean but do not say.

## What you will learn

- The six main kinds of reading question and how to spot each one.
- A step-by-step method for answering any reading question: read the question, read the text, predict, eliminate, check.
- How to pace yourself so you finish every passage, and what to do when time is running out.
- The traps that make wrong options look right.

## How these questions work

Almost every reading question fits one of six shapes. Learn to name the shape as soon as you read the question — it tells you where to look and what kind of answer to expect.

| Question shape | Typical wording | What it wants |
|---|---|---|
| Fact-finding | "According to the passage…" | Something the text says directly |
| Main idea and purpose | "The passage is mainly about…", "The writer's main purpose is…" | The big point, or why it was written |
| Inference | "It can be inferred that…", "Which is most likely true?" | Something the text shows but does not say |
| Vocabulary in context | "In paragraph 2, the word 'brittle' means…" | The meaning of a word in that sentence |
| Tone and technique | "The tone of the passage is…", "Why does the writer use a question?" | How the writer sounds, and the tools they use |
| Structure | "How does paragraph 2 relate to paragraph 1?" | How the parts of the text fit together |

A tiny example of each, using this sentence: *"Despite the drizzle, the stall-holders at the Sunday market were cheerful, and the queue for hot doughnuts snaked past the fountain."*

- **Fact-finding:** Where did the queue reach? (Past the fountain.)
- **Main idea:** What is the sentence mainly about? (A busy, cheerful market on a wet day.)
- **Inference:** Were the doughnuts popular? (Yes — the long queue shows it, even though the word "popular" is never used.)
- **Vocabulary:** What does "snaked" mean here? (Wound along in a long, bending line — not anything to do with real snakes.)
- **Tone:** How does the sentence sound? (Warm and lively.)
- **Structure:** What does "Despite" do? (It sets up a contrast: bad weather, but good mood.)

Watch for two special words in questions: **NOT** and **EXCEPT**. They flip the task — three options are true and you are hunting for the one that is false or not stated.

## Strategies

### Strategy 1: Pace yourself with checkpoints

In our practice tests you get 30 questions in 30 minutes, so you have about **one minute per question, including reading time**. If a passage has 6 questions, aim to finish it in about 6 minutes. Write the checkpoint times at the top of your working (for example, "Passage B done by minute 12") and glance at the clock when you finish each passage.

### Strategy 2: Read the questions first, then the passage

1. Skim the question stems (not the options) for the passage — about 15 seconds.
2. Read the passage once, carefully, holding those questions in mind.
3. Do not try to memorise details. You can always look back.

### Strategy 3: Predict, then eliminate

1. Read one question and cover the options with your hand or ruler.
2. Find the part of the text that answers it and **predict** the answer in your own words.
3. Uncover the options. Choose the one that matches your prediction.
4. If none matches, **eliminate**: prove each wrong option wrong. An option is wrong if it is not stated or shown, contradicts the text, is too broad, is too narrow, uses an extreme word the text does not support ("always", "never", "proved"), or is true but does not answer this question.

### Strategy 4: Point to the evidence

Before you mark an answer, put your finger on the words in the text that support it. If you cannot point to anything, you are probably choosing what you think or know, not what the text says.

### Strategy 5: Skip, flag, return, and never leave a blank

If a question is taking more than about 90 seconds, mark your best guess, flag it, and move on. Come back if there is time. A blank answer scores nothing, so — unless the instructions on the day say otherwise — make sure every question has an answer before time runs out.

## Worked examples

### Example 1

*The Wattle Creek Library lends more than books. Since last spring, members have been able to borrow seeds from a set of small wooden drawers near the front desk. Gardeners take a packet of beans, tomatoes or sunflowers, grow the plants at home, and at the end of the season return a packet of fresh seeds collected from their own crop. Librarian Mei Tan says the drawers have never been empty, because returned seeds now outnumber borrowed ones.*

According to the passage, why have the drawers never been empty?
A. The library buys new seeds every month. B. More seeds are returned than borrowed. C. Only members may borrow seeds. D. Gardeners grow only beans.

1. Name the shape: "According to the passage" — fact-finding. The answer is written in the text.
2. Find the place: the last sentence says the drawers have never been empty "because returned seeds now outnumber borrowed ones".
3. Predict: "people bring back more than they take".
4. Match: B says the same thing in different words.

**Answer: B.** The tempting wrong option is C: it is true (members borrow the seeds) but it does not explain why the drawers stay full.

### Example 2

*Bring your old mobile phones to Riverside Town Hall this Saturday between 9 am and noon. Volunteers will wipe any personal data and send the phones to be recycled, so the metals inside can be used again instead of ending up in landfill.*

The main purpose of this notice is to:
A. explain how phones are made. B. describe Riverside Town Hall. C. encourage people to bring old phones to a recycling event. D. entertain readers with a funny story.

1. Name the shape: "main purpose" — why was this written?
2. Predict: it tells readers where and when to bring phones, and gives a reason to do it. So it wants people to act.
3. Eliminate A: the notice says nothing about making phones.
4. Eliminate B: the Town Hall is only the place, not the subject.
5. Eliminate D: there is no story and nothing funny.

**Answer: C.** The tempting wrong option is B, because the hall is mentioned by name — but a detail is not the purpose.

### Example 3

*Jonah's soccer team had lost every match of the season. Before the final game, the coach moved Jonah from striker to goalkeeper. Jonah grumbled the whole warm-up. Then he saved two penalties, and afterwards he asked whether he could keep the gloves for next season.*

Which statement is best supported by the passage?
A. Jonah's team always loses. B. Jonah never wanted to play as a striker. C. The coach is unfair to Jonah. D. Jonah's feelings about playing in goal changed during the game.

1. Name the shape: "best supported" — an inference question. The answer must be backed by the text, not just possible.
2. Look for change: he "grumbled" at the start, but at the end he asked to keep the gloves.
3. Eliminate A: "always" is extreme. The team lost every match *of this season*, and we are not told the final result.
4. Eliminate B: the text never says how he felt about being a striker.
5. Eliminate C: the coach's choice worked out well; nothing says it was unfair.

**Answer: D.** The tempting wrong option is A, because the team had lost every match — but "always" goes further than the text.

## Common traps

- **True but not the answer.** The option repeats a real detail from the text but does not answer the question that was asked. Re-read the question stem before you choose.
- **Extreme words.** "Always", "never", "all", "proved" and "only" are wrong unless the text is just as strong.
- **Your own knowledge.** An option might be true in real life but not stated or shown in the passage. The passage is the only evidence that counts.
- **Missing NOT or EXCEPT.** Students who miss these words pick the first true option they see. Circle these words when they appear.
- **Spending too long on one passage.** Running out of time on the last passage costs more marks than one tricky question ever could.

## Tips to remember

- **"Read, Predict, Eliminate, Prove" (RPEP)** — a made-up memory trick for every question: read the stem, predict in your own words, eliminate the wrong options, prove your choice with words from the text.
- **"A minute a question."** With 30 questions in 30 minutes, a six-question passage gets about six minutes.
- **Be a detective, not a fortune-teller.** Detectives point to clues; fortune-tellers guess. Every answer needs a clue you can point to.
- **Too big, too small, just right.** For main idea questions, reject options that are too broad or too narrow — like Goldilocks.
- **No blanks.** Before time is up, every question has a letter.

## Key terms

- **Stem** — the question part of a multiple-choice item, before the options.
- **Option** — one of the possible answers (A, B, C or D).
- **Distractor** — a wrong option written to look tempting.
- **Evidence** — the words in the text that support an answer.
- **Elimination** — proving options wrong one by one until one is left.
- **Pacing** — sharing your time across the test so you reach every question.

## Summary

- Reading questions come in six main shapes: fact-finding, main idea and purpose, inference, vocabulary, tone and technique, and structure.
- Read the question stems first, then the passage, then answer one question at a time.
- Predict the answer before looking at the options, then eliminate options that are unsupported, extreme, too broad, too narrow or off-question.
- Point to evidence in the text for every answer.
- Keep to about one minute per question, skip and flag slow questions, and leave nothing blank.

questions.prompt: In a practice reading test with 30 questions and a time limit of 30 minutes, about how long should you allow for each question, including reading time?
questions.explanation: 30 minutes shared between 30 questions is 1 minute each, and that minute includes reading the passage. Two minutes each would need 60 minutes.
steps: Divide the time by the number of questions: 30 minutes ÷ 30 questions.
That gives 1 minute per question, including reading time.

mistakes.A: Pacing: 30 seconds each would only use 15 minutes — you have twice that. Divide 30 minutes by 30 questions.
mistakes.C: Pacing: 2 minutes each for 30 questions would need 60 minutes. Divide the total time by the number of questions.
mistakes.D: Pacing: 5 minutes is about the time for a whole six-question passage, not one question. Divide 30 by 30.

questions.prompt:
Read the passage.

On Saturday the Brookfield Primary fete raised money for new library shelves. The cake stall sold out by eleven o'clock, but the biggest earner was the second-hand book table, which took more money than the cake stall and the face-painting tent put together. The organisers plan to run the book table again next year.

According to the passage, which part of the fete earned the most money?
questions.explanation: The passage says directly that the biggest earner was the second-hand book table. The cake stall sold out, but selling out early does not mean it earned the most.
steps: This is a fact-finding question: the answer is stated in the passage.
Find the words 'the biggest earner' — they are followed by 'the second-hand book table'.

mistakes.A: True-but-not-the-answer trap: the cake stall sold out, but the passage says the book table earned more. Find the words 'biggest earner'.
mistakes.B: Detail trap: the face-painting tent is only mentioned to show how much the book table earned. Re-read the sentence with 'biggest earner'.
mistakes.D: Off-question trap: the shelves are what the money will buy, not a part of the fete that earned money.

questions.prompt: Which word in a question tells you that three of the options are true and you must find the one that is NOT?
questions.explanation: 'Except' (like 'NOT') flips the task: you look for the one option that is false or not stated. 'Best' and 'mainly' ask for the strongest true answer.
steps: Think about which words change the task from 'find the true one' to 'find the odd one out'.
'EXCEPT' and 'NOT' flip the task, so the answer is 'except'.

mistakes.A: 'Best' asks for the strongest correct answer, not the false one. Look for a word like NOT or EXCEPT.
mistakes.B: 'Mainly' signals a main idea question, not a 'find the false one' question.
mistakes.C: 'According to' signals a fact-finding question — the answer is stated in the text.

questions.prompt:
Read the passage.

Kiri had practised the piano piece for weeks, yet when she sat down at the school concert her hands felt as if they belonged to someone else. She missed the first chord. Then she noticed her grandfather in the front row, tapping the beat on his knee the way he always did at home. She matched her playing to his tapping, and by the final bar she was smiling.

What helped Kiri recover after her mistake?
questions.explanation: After the mistake she 'matched her playing to his tapping' — that is what got her back on track. Her weeks of practice are true, but they came before the mistake and did not stop it.
steps: Find the mistake in the passage ('She missed the first chord') and read what happens next.
She noticed her grandfather tapping the beat and 'matched her playing to his tapping', so his tapping helped her recover.

mistakes.B: True-but-not-the-answer trap: she did practise, but that happened before the concert and she still made the mistake. Look at what happened after it.
mistakes.C: This is the mistake itself, not what fixed it. Read the sentences after 'She missed the first chord'.
mistakes.D: Cause-and-effect mix-up: she was smiling at the end, as a result of recovering. It did not cause the recovery.

questions.prompt: With 6 minutes left in a reading test, you still have 9 questions to answer. Unless the instructions say otherwise, what is the most sensible plan?

options.A: Read the last passage very slowly so every answer is perfect
options.B: Answer the quickest questions first, then make a best guess on any left so none are blank
options.C: Leave the hardest questions blank so you do not lose marks
options.D: Go back and re-check your earlier answers instead

questions.explanation: With less than a minute per question, do the quick ones and then guess the rest — a blank scores nothing, and a guess might score. Reading very slowly would leave questions unanswered.
steps: 6 minutes for 9 questions is less than 1 minute each, so you cannot give every question full attention.
A blank answer scores nothing, so grab the quick marks first, then put a best guess on every question left.

mistakes.A: Pacing trap: reading slowly means some questions will be left with no answer at all. Get the quick marks first, then guess.
mistakes.C: Guessing trap: a blank always scores zero, but a guess has a chance. Unless the rules say otherwise, never leave a blank.
mistakes.D: Pacing trap: checking old answers while 9 questions are still empty throws away easy marks. Answer everything first.

questions.prompt:
Read the passage.

Five years ago, the laneways behind Ferris Street were grey and covered in scribbled tags. The council then invited local artists to paint murals on the walls. Today the lanes are bright with painted birds, rivers and portraits of local people, and shop owners say far more visitors walk through them. Some cafés have even opened their back doors onto the lanes.

Which sentence best states the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Local artists like to paint birds and rivers.
options.B: Art is important in every town in the world.
options.C: Painting murals has turned unloved laneways into places people want to visit.
options.D: Scribbled tags are a problem for councils.

questions.explanation: The whole passage moves from grey, tagged lanes to bright lanes that attract visitors and cafés, so C covers it. A is only one detail — too narrow.
steps: Main idea questions need an option that covers the whole passage — not too broad, not too narrow.
The passage describes the lanes before, the murals, and the result (more visitors, cafés opening onto the lanes), which is what C says.

mistakes.A: Too narrow: birds and rivers are just examples of what was painted. The main idea must cover the whole passage.
mistakes.B: Too broad: the passage is about one set of laneways, not every town in the world.
mistakes.D: Detail trap: the tags are only the starting point. The passage is about how the lanes changed.

questions.prompt:
Read the passage.

The Ellery footbridge opened in 1932, linking the flour mill on the north bank to the workers' cottages on the south bank. Made of timber, it was rebuilt twice after floods, and in 1998 it was replaced by a steel bridge wide enough for bicycles. A small plaque at the south end still lists the names of the eleven carpenters who built the first bridge.

Which of these is NOT stated in the passage?

options.A: The first bridge was made of timber.
options.B: The bridge linked a mill to workers' cottages.
options.C: The steel bridge is wide enough for bicycles.
options.D: The carpenters lived in the workers' cottages.

questions.explanation: The passage names the carpenters on a plaque but never says where they lived, so D is not stated. A, B and C can each be pointed to in the text.
steps: This is a NOT question: three options are stated and one is not. Check each one against the text.
'Made of timber' (A), 'linking the flour mill… to the workers' cottages' (B) and 'wide enough for bicycles' (C) are all in the text.
Nothing says where the carpenters lived, so D is the one that is not stated.

mistakes.A: Missed-NOT trap: this IS stated ('Made of timber'). You need the option the passage does not say.
mistakes.B: Missed-NOT trap: this IS stated in the first sentence. Find the option you cannot point to.
mistakes.C: Missed-NOT trap: this IS stated ('wide enough for bicycles'). Find the option with no evidence in the text.

questions.prompt:
Read the passage. The sentences are numbered.

(1) Dad said the old caravan would be 'an adventure'. (2) The door had to be lifted before it would close, and the tap coughed brown water for a full minute. (3) On the first night, rain drummed on the roof and dripped into a saucepan Dad had placed on the bench. (4) Even so, when the sun rose over the lake, Leo admitted it was the best view he had ever woken up to.

Which sentence best shows that Leo's attitude to the trip changed?
questions.explanation: 'Even so… Leo admitted' shows Leo now likes something about the trip despite the problems — 'admitted' suggests he had not expected to. Sentence 1 gives Dad's opinion, not Leo's.
steps: The question is about Leo's attitude changing, so look for Leo's feelings, not the caravan's problems.
Sentences 2 and 3 describe problems; sentence 1 is Dad's view.
Sentence 4 begins 'Even so' and says Leo 'admitted' it was the best view — a change in how he felt.

mistakes.B: Wrong-person trap: sentence 1 is what Dad thought, not Leo. The question asks about Leo.
mistakes.C: Off-question trap: sentence 2 shows the caravan was in poor condition, not that Leo's feelings changed.
mistakes.D: Off-question trap: sentence 3 describes the leaking roof. Look for a sentence about how Leo feels.

questions.prompt:
Read the passage.

Mrs Okafor's Year 7 class tested whether students remembered more spelling words when they wrote them by hand or typed them. Over three weeks, the handwriting group remembered slightly more words on average, although a few typists scored higher than some of the handwriters. Mrs Okafor said the class should repeat the test with more students before deciding anything.

Which statement is best supported by the passage?

options.A: Typing never helps students remember spelling words.
options.B: In this small test, the handwriting group did a little better on average.
options.C: Every student who wrote by hand beat every student who typed.
options.D: The class proved that handwriting is the best way to learn spelling.

questions.explanation: The passage says the handwriting group remembered 'slightly more words on average' — exactly B. D is tempting, but the teacher says they should test again 'before deciding anything', so nothing was proved.
steps: Look for an option that says no more than the text says. Watch for extreme words like 'never', 'every' and 'proved'.
The text says the handwriting group remembered slightly more on average, but some typists did better and the result is not final — which matches B.

mistakes.A: Extreme-word trap: 'never' is far stronger than the text. The typists still remembered words, and some beat handwriters.
mistakes.C: Contradiction trap: the passage says a few typists scored higher than some handwriters.
mistakes.D: Extreme-word trap: 'proved' is too strong — Mrs Okafor wants to repeat the test before deciding anything.

questions.prompt:
Read the passage.

When the storm cut the power, the Nguyen family dug out the board games. At first Thao complained that she would miss the final episode of her favourite show. By nine o'clock, though, she was the one begging for 'just one more round', even after the lights had flickered back on.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?

options.A: Thao no longer cares about her favourite show.
options.B: The power stayed off all evening.
options.C: Thao enjoyed the games more than she had expected to.
options.D: Thao wanted to keep playing because the lights were still off.

questions.explanation: She complained at first but later begged for one more round, so she enjoyed the games more than she expected. A goes too far — one evening of fun does not show she no longer cares about the show.
steps: Compare Thao at the start ('complained') with Thao at nine o'clock ('begging for just one more round').
Check the tempting options: the lights came back on (so B and D are contradicted), and nothing says she stopped caring about the show (A overreaches).
The change from complaining to begging supports C.

mistakes.A: Over-inference trap: enjoying one game night does not prove she stopped caring about her show. Choose the option the text fully supports.
mistakes.B: Contradiction trap: the passage says the lights 'flickered back on'. Re-read the last sentence.
mistakes.D: Contradiction trap: she kept asking to play even after the lights were back on, so the power was not the reason.

questions.prompt: In a practice test, Sam answered the first two passages almost perfectly but left the last 8 questions blank because time ran out. He spent 16 minutes on the first passage alone. Which change would most likely raise his score?

options.A: Read every passage twice so he makes fewer mistakes
options.B: Answer the questions without reading the passages, to save time
options.C: Spend even longer on the first passage so it is perfect
options.D: Set a checkpoint time for each passage, move on when it passes, and guess any question still blank at the end

questions.explanation: Sam's problem is pacing, not accuracy: 8 blanks cost him up to 8 marks. Checkpoints keep him moving, and guessing the leftovers means none score zero for being blank. Reading twice would make the time problem worse.
steps: Work out what is costing Sam marks: he is accurate, but 8 questions got no answer at all.
So he needs a pacing fix. Of the options, only D keeps him moving (checkpoints) and fills in any blanks (guessing).

mistakes.A: Pacing trap: reading twice uses even more time, so even more questions would be left blank. His problem is time, not accuracy.
mistakes.B: Shortcut trap: skipping the reading would wreck his accuracy. He needs to manage time per passage, not stop reading.
mistakes.C: Pacing trap: he already spends far too long on passage one (16 minutes). More time there means more blanks later.

questions.prompt:
Read the passage.

For centuries, sailors crossed open ocean by watching the stars. On a clear night, a skilled navigator could judge direction from just a few familiar stars low on the horizon.

Cloudy weather, however, left sailors guessing. A single overcast week could push a ship far off course, which is why better instruments for finding direction and position mattered so much to sailors.

How does the second paragraph relate to the first?

options.A: It explains a weakness of the method described in the first paragraph.
options.B: It gives another example of the same method.
options.C: It argues that the stars were never useful for navigation.
options.D: It tells the story of one particular sailor.

questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 describes navigating by stars; paragraph 2 begins with 'however' and explains that clouds made this method fail. C is too extreme — paragraph 2 says the method failed in cloudy weather, not that it was never useful.
steps: Look at the linking word at the start of paragraph 2: 'however' signals a contrast or problem.
Paragraph 2 shows when star navigation did not work (cloudy weather) and why that mattered — a weakness of the method in paragraph 1.

mistakes.B: Structure trap: paragraph 2 does not describe star navigation working; 'however' introduces a problem with it.
mistakes.C: Extreme-word trap: 'never useful' contradicts paragraph 1, which says the stars worked on clear nights.
mistakes.D: Detail trap: no single sailor is named or followed; the passage talks about sailors in general.
